title: Stochastic Similarity Renormalization Group
authors: Rongzhe Hu, Xin Zhen, Furong Xu, Junchen Pei
abstract: By integrating the quantum Monte Carlo technique into the similarity renormalization group (SRG), we have developed a stochastic SRG framework (SRGQMC) capable of both free-space two-body and in-medium many-body evolutions. This approach circumvents the combinatorial tensor-space explosion of many-body flow equations by mapping continuous unitary transformations onto an ensemble of signed random walkers. We benchmark the SRGQMC against deterministic free-space SRG evolutions of realistic nucleon-nucleon (NN) interactions, as well as against in-medium SRG (IMSRG) many-body calculations with the Richardson pairing model at two- and three-body levels [IMSRG(2)/(3)]. While a deterministic extension to the four-body level [IMSRG(4)] remains unfeasible due to prohibitive computational costs, we have achieved the first IMSRG(4) calculation by using the stochastic technique, demonstrating a substantial improvement toward the full configuration-interaction limit. This stochastic framework provides a practical pathway to higher-order IMSRG calculations.
summary: This work introduces the Stochastic Similarity Renormalization Group (SRGQMC) method, which uses Quantum Monte Carlo techniques to simulate continuous unitary transformations in nuclear physics. It successfully bypasses the prohibitive computational cost of high-order In-Medium SRG calculations by sampling operator flow stochastically. This allows for reliable predictions up to four-body correlations, significantly advancing our understanding of strongly interacting quantum matter.
main_problem: Developing a scalable method for high-order In-Medium Similarity Renormalization Group (IMSRG) calculations that overcomes the combinatorial tensor-space explosion associated with traditional deterministic flow equations.
main_result: The stochastic framework successfully achieves the first IMSRG(4) calculation, demonstrating significant improvement in convergence toward the Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) limit compared to lower-order truncations.
method: It introduces Stochastic Similarity Renormalization Group with Quantum Monte Carlo (SRGQMC), which maps continuous unitary flow equations onto an ensemble of signed random walkers to sample commutator structures instead of evolving full operator matrices.
model_or_system: The calculations are applied to nuclear many-body systems, using the Richardson pairing model for testing. The underlying physics involves evolving Hamiltonians via a continuous unitary transformation governed by flow equations up to four-body operators.
key_observables: Correlation energy ($E_{	ext{corr}}$), free-space scattering phase shifts, and comparison of calculated values against deterministic IMSRG orders ($	ext{IMSRG}(2)$ through $	ext{IMSRG}(4)$) and the exact FCI limit.
important_parameters: Coupling strength ($g$), flow parameter ($s$), walker population ($N_w$), and number of stochastic loops ($N_{	ext{loop}}$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that mapping the deterministic flow onto a stochastic ensemble provides an unbiased estimate, which is confirmed by observing convergence as $N_w$ or $N_{	ext{loop}}$ increases.
figures_summary: Figures compare SRG/SRGQMC evolved NN interaction matrix elements and phase shifts; another compares correlation energy vs. pairing strength for different IMSRG orders; a third shows the evolution of $E_{	ext{corr}}(s)$ tracking deterministic calculations.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need to overcome tensor-space explosion in high-order IMSRG. It then details the SRGQMC formalism, applying it first to free-space NN interactions and subsequently to the pairing model, culminating in the demonstration of $	ext{IMSRG}(4)$ feasibility.
why_interesting: The stochastic approach provides a powerful computational tool for simulating complex many-body quantum dynamics where deterministic tensor contractions become intractable due to exponential scaling.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. SRG- and SRGQMC-evolved neutron-proton interactions at λ = 2.0 fm−1 for N3LOEMN(500). Columns from left to right denote the 1S0, 3P0, 3S1, 3D1, and ϵ1 channels. Row 2 presents the SRGQMC-evolved matrix elements V (p′, p) using the stochastic loop-averaged sampling with Nw = 104 and Nloop = 10. Row 3 shows the scattering phase shifts (including the mixing angle ϵ1) against the laboratory energy Tlab, derived from SRG (blue solid lines) and SRGQMC (red dots with error bars), compared with the empirical Nijmegen analysis (open diamonds) [22] as a reference.

FIG. 2. Correlation energy of the A = 4 Richardson pair- ing Hamiltonian as a function of the pairing strength g. The deterministic IMSRG(2), IMSRG(3) and FCI results are com- pared with SRGQMC(2), SRGQMC(3) and SRGQMC(4) cal- culations. Error bars denote the statistical uncertainties from independent stochastic loops. The FCI result is obtained by directly diagonalizing the Hamiltonian in the specified model space.

FIG. 3. SRGQMC flow of the correlation energy for the A = 4 Richardson pairing Hamiltonian at g = 1.0 MeV. Shaded bands indicate statistical uncertainties. Deterministic IM- SRG(2), IMSRG(3) and FCI results are shown on the right axis by black dots.

FIG. 1. Convergence of the calculated phase shifts with respect to the walker population Nw. Three rows correspond to Nw = 102, 103, and 104, respectively, with Nloop = 10 fixed. Columns show the 1S0, 3P0, 3S1, 3D1, and ϵ1 channels for the N3LOEMN(500) interaction evolved to λ = 2.0 fm−1. Solid curves denote deterministic SRG results, red points with error bars denote SRGQMC results, and open diamonds show the Nijmegen phase-shift analysis as an empirical reference.

FIG. 2. Convergence of the Richardson pairing-model correlation energy with respect to Nw. Columns correspond to g = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0 MeV. The three rows show SRGQMC(2), SRGQMC(3), and SRGQMC(4), respectively. Dashed horizontal lines denote the corresponding deterministic IMSRG(2), IMSRG(3) and IMSRG(4) values, the last of which is equivalent to the exact FCI for the present A = 4 system.
